title: THE BIBLE ACTUALLY COMMANDS PEOPLE TO BURY THEIR EXCREMENT—AND THE REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN STOP AND THINK.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE ACTUALLY COMMANDS PEOPLE TO BURY THEIR EXCREMENT—AND THE REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN STOP AND THINK.

Buried in Deuteronomy 23:12–14 is one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable commands. But behind the dirt, the shovel, and the shocking connection to God’s presence lies a truth about holiness, hidden sin, and the grace of Jesus Christ that we desperately need to hear.
There are Bible verses people love to frame on their walls.
“For God so loved the world…”
“The LORD is my shepherd…”
“I can do all things through Christ…”
And then there is Deuteronomy 23:12–14.
The passage nobody is putting on a coffee mug.
The passage that talks about human excrement.
Yes. Actual human waste.
And not as a metaphor.
God literally commanded the Israelites to go outside their military camp, relieve themselves, dig a hole, and cover what they left behind.
You might laugh.
You might wonder why something so unpleasant deserves a place in Holy Scripture.
The God who spoke to Moses about His glory, His covenant, and His holiness also cared about what His people did with their waste.
And the reason He gave is far more serious than you might imagine.
Because this strange command ends with a warning about the presence of God.
Not simply about cleanliness.
Not merely about avoiding an unpleasant smell.
About the Holy One walking among His people.
And once you understand what was happening in that ancient camp, you may begin to see something about your own life that is much harder to ignore than a pile of dirt.
Listen to the words of Scripture.

“You shall have a place also without the camp, where you shall go forth abroad: And you shall have a paddle upon your weapon; and it shall be, when you will ease yourself abroad, you shall dig therewith, and shall turn back and cover that which comes from you: For the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you, and to give up your enemies before you; therefore shall your camp be holy: that he see no unclean thing in you, and turn away from you.”
— Deuteronomy 23:12–14, translated from the Hebrew; compare the King James Version.
Read that final reason again.
“For the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp.”
Imagine being there.

The wilderness stretches beyond the horizon. The ground is dry beneath your sandals. Tents stand in rows. Soldiers prepare their weapons. Families remember the deliverance of their ancestors from Egypt.
They are not simply a collection of travelers.
They are a covenant people.
The God who delivered Israel from slavery has chosen to dwell among them.
And this changes everything.
Even the ordinary.
Even the unpleasant.
Even the things people would rather never discuss.
In the Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 23:14, we encounter the words:
כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ מִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּקֶרֶב מַחֲנֶךָ
Ki YHWH Elohekha mithallekh beqerev machanekha.
“For the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp.”
The Hebrew verb mithallekh comes from the root הלך (halakh), meaning “to walk” or “to go.” Here, its grammatical form portrays God as moving about within the camp.
The language emphasizes His active presence among His people.
The camp was not merely a military installation.
It was a place where the covenant Lord was present to protect and deliver Israel.
That is why the next phrase matters.
וְהָיָה מַחֲנֶיךָ קָדוֹשׁ
Vehayah machanekha qadosh.
“And your camp shall be holy.”
The word qadosh means holy, set apart, or consecrated.
God's presence required His people to recognize that their camp belonged to Him.
And that holiness had implications for how they lived.
Including their sanitation.
Think about that.
The same God who commanded Israel not to murder, steal, or worship idols also gave instructions for handling bodily waste.
Why?
Because holiness was never supposed to be a religious performance reserved for sacred ceremonies.
Israel's covenant life was to acknowledge God in ordinary daily conduct.
Their worship and their behavior belonged together.
But there is something important we must understand before turning this passage into a sermon about hidden sin.
Deuteronomy 23:12–14 is first and foremost a literal instruction about camp sanitation and ritual propriety.
The Hebrew expression ervat davar (עֶרְוַת דָּבָר), translated in this context as something indecent or offensive, belongs to the language of what was inappropriate within Israel's holy camp.
It would be inaccurate to claim that human excrement itself was a moral sin or that every bodily function was spiritually evil.
God created the human body.
Its normal functions are not inherently sinful.
The command concerned the appropriate handling of waste in a camp set apart for God's presence.
It also had practical hygienic benefits, even though the passage explicitly grounds the command in holiness and God's presence rather than in a modern explanation of disease prevention.
This distinction matters.
Because faithful preaching must never make Scripture say what Scripture does not say.
Yet the passage does reveal a profound biblical principle.
The presence of a holy God matters in the ordinary details of human life.
And that principle reaches far beyond an ancient wilderness camp.
It reaches into the way we live when nobody is watching.
Into the choices we make when there is no audience.
Into the gap between the person we present to the world and the person we actually are.
And this is where the laughter begins to fade.
Because while most of us would never leave human waste exposed in the middle of our living room, we can become remarkably comfortable leaving destructive things unaddressed within our hearts.
We know how to clean a house before visitors arrive.
We know how to dress appropriately for church.
We know how to smile when someone asks how we are doing.
We know how to say, “God is good,” even when our private life is falling apart.
But sometimes we have no idea how to tell another believer that we are struggling.
Sometimes the anger has been growing for years.
Sometimes the pornography has become a secret habit.
Sometimes bitterness has become so familiar that we no longer recognize it.
Sometimes pride disguises itself as spiritual maturity.
Sometimes the person posting Bible verses online is also the person desperately hoping nobody discovers what happened last night.
And sometimes the hardest words to say are not “Praise the Lord.”
They are:
“Lord, I have sinned.”
“Lord, I need help.”
“Lord, I cannot keep pretending.”
Now, we must be careful.
Deuteronomy does not teach that literal waste represents every hidden sin. The passage does not establish a universal rule that Christians must bury their mistakes to keep God nearby.
But when we read this law within the whole testimony of Scripture, we encounter a consistent truth.
God's holiness is not a costume we put on for religious occasions.
And our response to His holiness must involve more than appearances.
David understood this after his devastating moral failure.
He had committed adultery with Bathsheba.
He had arranged circumstances that led to the death of her husband, Uriah.
He had tried to manage the consequences of his actions.
For a time, the truth remained concealed from public view.
But hidden from people does not mean hidden from God.
When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David could no longer maintain the illusion.
His confession eventually gave us one of the most heartbreaking prayers in Scripture.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
— Psalm 51:10, KJV
Notice what David asked for.
Not a better reputation.
Not a more convincing explanation.
Not a way to silence everyone who knew what he had done.
A clean heart.
Because there comes a moment when managing the appearance of righteousness becomes more exhausting than confessing the truth.
Maybe you know that exhaustion.
Maybe you are reading this with a struggle you have never told anyone.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
Your friends think you are fine.
Your church thinks you have everything together.
But you know the truth.
There are nights when you stare at the ceiling, wondering how someone who loves Jesus can still struggle so deeply.
There are prayers you start but cannot finish.
There are memories that return without warning.
There are things you wish you could undo.
And perhaps you have wondered whether God has grown tired of you.
Here is where the Gospel must interrupt our fear.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had already made itself clean. He came because sinners needed a Savior.
This is the difference between merely using an Old Testament command as a moral lesson and reading the Bible through the fulfillment of God's redemptive purposes in Christ.
Under the Mosaic covenant, Israel received instructions governing the holiness of its camp.
Those instructions belonged to a larger system of covenant life, purity, worship, and divine presence.
But the New Testament announces something extraordinary.
The eternal Son of God entered our world.
John writes:
— John 1:14, KJV
The Greek word translated “dwelt” is ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen).
It comes from a verb meaning to pitch a tent or dwell in a tabernacle.
John's language powerfully recalls God's dwelling among His people.
In the wilderness, God was present among Israel.
In Jesus Christ, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
The holy God did not remain distant from humanity's brokenness.
He came near.
And look at whom Jesus approached.
A leper whose condition had isolated him from ordinary community life.
A tax collector despised by his neighbors.
A woman whose history made her the subject of public discussion.
A criminal dying beside Him.
People whose lives were marked by shame, exclusion, guilt, or suffering.
Jesus did not treat all their circumstances as identical.
He did not call evil good.
He did not suggest repentance was unnecessary.
But neither did He refuse to extend mercy to those who desperately needed Him.
In Mark 1:40–42, a man with leprosy approached Jesus and pleaded:
“If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.”
Jesus reached out and touched him.
And said:
“I will; be thou clean.”
The Greek words are unforgettable.
θέλω, καθαρίσθητι
Thelō, katharisthēti.
“I am willing; be cleansed.”
The man did not cleanse himself before approaching Christ.
He came to the One who could cleanse him.
And Jesus responded with compassion and power.
Do you see the beauty?
The holiness of Jesus was not overcome by the man's uncleanness.
Instead, Jesus cleansed him.

That miracle does not mean physical disease is equivalent to personal sin. It reveals Christ's authority and compassion toward someone suffering under a condition that carried significant social and ritual consequences.
And it points us toward an even greater hope.
The Savior who can cleanse the unclean is also the Savior who forgives sinners.
But forgiveness is not pretending sin never mattered.
Forgiveness was purchased at a terrible cost.
At the cross, Jesus bore our sins.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The sinless Son of God gave Himself for people who could never purchase their own redemption.
Peter writes:
— 1 Peter 2:24, KJV
The cross is not God's declaration that sin is harmless.
It is the clearest demonstration of how seriously God takes sin and how astonishingly far His love has gone to save sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Your darkness does not matter.”
It says, “Your darkness is not greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.”
And that changes the story.
Because the person who has spent years hiding does not have to remain hidden.
The believer trapped in recurring sin can confess, seek accountability, and walk toward genuine repentance.
The wounded person who has mistaken another person's cruelty for God's character can begin to rediscover His goodness.
The Christian who has fallen can return to the Lord.
Not because repentance earns salvation.
But because the grace that saves us also teaches us to turn away from sin.
Titus 2:11–12 explains that God's saving grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not give sin permission to reign.
Grace breaks sin's claim to be our master.
And here is another beautiful connection.
In 1 Corinthians 6:19, Paul asks believers:
“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?”
In the Greek, the word ναός (naos) refers to a temple or sacred dwelling place.
Paul is addressing believers about honoring God with their bodies, particularly in the context of sexual morality.
Elsewhere, in 1 Corinthians 3:16–17, he describes the gathered church as God's temple.
These passages do not simply reproduce the sanitation laws of Deuteronomy.
They reveal how the reality of God's presence among His people is understood under the new covenant.
God's Spirit dwells among and within those who belong to Christ.
That should awaken reverence.
Not panic.
Not superstition.
Not the terrifying idea that every intrusive thought, weakness, or ordinary bodily function drives the Holy Spirit away.
Believers are called to holiness because they belong to Christ.
And when they sin, they are called to confess and return to Him rather than hide in despair.
John gives us this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9, KJV
There it is.
That word again.
Cleanse.
Not conceal.
Not excuse.
Not pretend.
Cleanse.
Maybe that is the word you needed today.
Because somewhere along the way, you began to believe that God only wanted the polished version of you.
The version who never doubts.
Never struggles.
Never feels tempted.
Never becomes angry.
Never cries in the bathroom so nobody hears.
Never wakes up ashamed of yesterday.
But the Lord already knows the truth about you.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not to deceive Him with a cleaner appearance.
It is to come to Him through Jesus Christ.
With repentance.
With faith.
With an honest heart.
The cross is sufficient for sins too serious to excuse.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
That is why we must not misunderstand the warning in Deuteronomy.
When God told Israel that He must not see something indecent in their camp and turn away, He was addressing the holiness required of His covenant people in their historical setting.
It would be wrong to tell a struggling Christian that one failure automatically makes Christ abandon them.
Jesus Himself said:
“And him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37, KJV
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus…”
Those are not invitations to treat sin casually.
They are reasons to stop running from the Savior.
Repentance is not an attempt to convince a reluctant Jesus to love us.
It is the proper response of a sinner to the mercy and truth revealed in Him.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing in your spiritual life is not the sin you are ashamed to confess.
Perhaps it is the belief that you must keep hiding it because grace could never reach someone like you.
That belief is not the Gospel.
Jesus died for sinners.
And sinners are exactly the people He calls to repentance.
So what do we do with this strange passage about burying excrement?
We read it faithfully.
We recognize its original meaning.
We respect its place in Israel's covenant life.
We refuse to twist it into a claim that human bodies are disgusting or that God is offended by normal physical functions.
We learn that the Lord's presence called Israel to holiness even in the practical details of daily life.
And then, through the fuller revelation of Scripture, we remember that Jesus Christ came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish through their own efforts.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A transformed life.
A future that is no longer defined by the worst thing we have done.
That is the heart of From Scandal to Grace.
Not that scandal is insignificant.
Not that consequences magically disappear.
Not that every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But that Jesus Christ can redeem people whose lives have been shattered by sin, shame, failure, and grief.
He can transform the proud into the humble.
The dishonest into the truthful.
The cruel into the compassionate.
The enslaved into people learning to walk in freedom.
The spiritually dead into those made alive by grace.
And sometimes the beginning of that transformation is painfully simple.
An honest confession.
A prayer whispered through tears.
A decision to seek help.
An apology without excuses.
A habit finally brought into the light.
A return to Scripture after months of spiritual numbness.
A trembling surrender to Jesus Christ.
Not every struggle disappears overnight.
Sanctification is often a lifelong journey.
But the believer does not walk that journey alone.
The same Savior who calls us to follow Him also promises His presence.
And that brings us to a question.
What would change in your life if you truly lived with the awareness that you belong to Jesus Christ?
Not merely when you enter a church building.
Not merely when you post a verse online.
Not merely when someone asks you to pray.
But when you are alone.
When you are tempted.
When you are angry.
When you are deciding whether to tell the truth.
When forgiveness feels impossible.
When you are exhausted from fighting a battle nobody else can see.
Would you keep pretending?
Or would you finally bring that struggle before the Lord?
If this message has touched a place you rarely talk about, you do not need to reveal private details publicly. But you can make a simple, honest confession of dependence on God's grace.
Someone else may need to hear that failure does not have to be the end of their story.
There is a person on your Facebook friends list who looks perfectly fine.
They smile in their photographs.
They celebrate birthdays.
They post about work, family, and ordinary life.
But perhaps they are privately struggling with shame.
Perhaps they have stopped praying because they believe they have disappointed God too many times.
Perhaps they are one quiet moment away from believing they are beyond forgiveness.
You may never know.
Not to shame anyone.
Not to embarrass someone into repentance.
But to put the truth of the Gospel within reach of people who may be too afraid to ask for help.
Here, we want to keep pointing people beyond appearances, beyond empty religious language, and back to the living Word of God.
Not toward a personality.
Not toward a platform.
Toward Jesus Christ.
And if you believe this kind of Scripture-centered ministry matters, there is another meaningful way you can help.
Every article requires time spent studying Scripture, examining context, checking translations, writing, and preparing resources that can help people understand the Gospel more deeply.
As Paul writes:
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Your first responsibility is to follow Christ faithfully and steward what He has entrusted to you wisely.
Supporting your local church, caring for your family, and helping people in need are deeply important expressions of Christian stewardship.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement for daily devotion, or thoughtful gifts that point others toward Christ.
But the greatest reason to join is not merchandise.
It is the opportunity to participate in a ministry committed to biblical truth, Gospel-centered encouragement, discipleship, and the hope of redemption through Jesus.
And remember, you do not have to pay to begin growing in the Word.
We want people to encounter Scripture whether they can afford to give or not.
It is about making the truth of Jesus Christ known.
About reaching the believer who is barely holding on.
About reminding the repentant sinner that forgiveness is real.
About helping the spiritually hungry discover the riches of God's Word.
About pointing a world full of carefully managed appearances toward the Savior who knows the truth about us and still calls sinners to come to Him.
Think back to that ancient wilderness camp.
A shovel.
A hole in the ground.
An ordinary, unpleasant human necessity.
And a holy God who cared about the conduct of His covenant people.
Who would have expected a passage about burying excrement to lead us into such a serious conversation about God's presence?
Yet Scripture has a way of confronting our assumptions.
The things we consider too ordinary for God may still belong within our obedience to Him.
The sins we try hardest to conceal are the very things we need to confess.
And the broken lives we consider beyond restoration may become testimonies to the power of His grace.
If you have been hiding from God, hear the invitation of Jesus.
Come to Him.
Not with an invented story about your righteousness.
Not with excuses for what you know is wrong.
But with repentance and faith.
You do not have to make yourself worthy of the cross.
You cannot.
That is why Christ came.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day.
That is the Gospel proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And it is the reason your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
So tonight, before you close your eyes, perhaps you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, You know the things I have tried to hide. You know my failures, my fears, and the places where I have resisted Your truth. Forgive me. Give me a heart that loves what is holy. Teach me to repent without despair and to receive Your grace without treating sin lightly. Help me walk honestly before You. Strengthen me through Your Word, Your Spirit, and the fellowship of Your people. Let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen.”
And when tomorrow comes, remember this:
The God who cared about the cleanliness of Israel's wilderness camp is the same holy God whose saving grace has been revealed to us in Jesus Christ.
His holiness has not diminished.
His mercy has not run dry.
And His invitation to repent and believe the Gospel still stands.
You may have spent years trying to bury the evidence of your brokenness, but Jesus came to bring the broken person into the light of His redeeming grace.
